en: From the pampered woman.
Chachykey’s white palace
Had a gate of solid iron and tin;
The pampered daughter-in-law’s
Splendor was exceedingly great.
No one dared approach it,
And whoever did was amazed;
No traveler dared go there,
And whoever looked was amazed.
At Chachykey’s encampment,
Acting as mediators there,
The three senior wives entered
To learn what had become
Of the falcon that had flown away.
Körpöjan, wife of Khan Bakay,
Moved like a goose with young,
Walked inside, and began speaking:
“You were once a younger child;
Ah, delight who shares my life!
Now, my child, tell the truth.
They opened their horses’ stride;
Along the shore of Ala-Köl,
Prince Semetey the lion
Lost Akshunkar.
Take wisdom worth red gold;
My precious child, heed my words!
We followed the chain of tradition,
Asked the learned men,
And heard words from men of counsel:
My colt, we heard that you know
Of the falcon that was carried away.
Ah, my colt Chachykey,
Tell the song you have sung,
And speak your secret faithfully!
If you tell your secret, you will prosper
And become a pure senior wife.
If you are human, tell the truth:
How did you sleep, and what dream did you see?
What manner of event did you witness?
Tell the truth, my colt!
Think upon what came before and after;
If you do not tell it, your blue lord
May mock you for nothing.
A man’s work is solid iron,
My child, but your name is woman;
One needs skill to melt it.
If you do not tell, shame and reproach
Will fall upon your own head.
If you do not tell, my colt,
What can I say of every deed
Of your dark-hearted prince,
The true son of the tiger,
Descendant of the mighty
Who smoked whenever he was spent
And grew fiercer whenever he died?
If you do not tell, suddenly,
When that desperate man’s anger rises,
A man’s affairs are perilous.
May he not stretch out the hair at your temples,
Or give you the divorce of a cast-off wife!
Do not be obstinate; hear my words.
My daughter-in-law, heed me now.
If you disobey and your sorrow boils,
He may put a kementei upon you,
Mount you on a bay mare,
And drive you toward your father.
When your father gave you,
When you came here as a bride,
You shone in a kete coat,
Rode proudly upon a bay pacer,
And shone in a supa coat,
And rode proudly on a gray pacer.
If you make trouble, my colt,
How will you depart,
Flapping in a kementei,
Swaggering on a bay mare?
Know that this would be a great shame.
How will you wander away,
Swaggering on a gray mare,
Flapping in a hide coat?
My child, heed these words of mine:
All the people blessed by Kydyr are here;
Dear old Bakay is here;
Sarykan of the bowl-shaped eyes,
The khan of sacred power, is here;
And Jamgyrchy, hero of the Esheks,
Is also here.”
When the senior wife said this,
The witless woman Chachykey
Now stood and seethed,
And spoke in an altogether different way
To the khans of the Esheks:
“Women who came as mediators,
Leave now, you wretches!
Dig your deep graves—
I shall boil your suffering!
You came here seeking support
From your sprawling elder Bakay.
I know all of you perfectly:
Your white-bearded old Bakay,
You three women, his playthings,
And your hairless bald man
Whom you sit worshiping as a saint.
I know what you are doing,
And the one you chose to bring,
Your witless, lowborn fellow
Called Jamgyrchy.
May God strike down
All you old ones with swan-white beards!”
The poor woman did not know
That Bakay was listening nearby;
Beginning with Khan Bakay,
She cursed every one of them.
The three senior wives led the way
And fled outside in a rush,
Their necks stretching like geese,
Both cheeks turning red.
There was no cure to be found:
“She has insulted the khan,” they said,
And all pinched their own faces.
Old Bakay heard
Her vicious torrent of abuse,
And all that had been said.
Misery fell upon Bakay.
The three khans sat drooping,
Hunched like frozen camels,
Unable to die from shame,
Or enter the grave in death,
Unable to understand
What manner of woman this loud daughter-in-law was.
Since Bakay first became Bakay,
Since Bakay first mounted a horse,
Since he stretched himself and became a man,
Standing equal with the sons of heroes,
Since Bakay first mounted a horse
And became a pillar of the people,
He had never died when fate reached him;
Bakay was no woman,
Yet he had never seen such treatment from a man.
To witness this judgment-day affair,
To have his beard and head reviled—
It was the death of Khan Bakay.
Prince Bakay the tiger,
Who had mustered armies and struck the Kalmyks,
Your elder Prince Bakay,
Broke down and spoke in a low voice:
“In the time when our fortune remained safe,
When the tiger Manas lived,
Kara-Shaar and Kambyl—
